analysis.one_liner: Allows importation of cheaper prescription drugs from Canada and other approved countries, with safety rules and tax penalties for manufacturers that block them.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by the Senate Finance Committee's own chairman, never received a hearing, vote, or a single cosponsor, and expired when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten federal drug law to let licensed U.S. pharmacists, wholesalers, and individuals buy prescription drugs from registered exporters in Canada and, eventually, other developed countries, where the same medicines often sell for far less. It paired that with safety machinery — exporter registration, FDA monitoring, chain-of-custody verification, and shipment markings — and with tax pressure on drug makers: companies that tried to stop or discourage importation would lose their advertising tax deduction, while those that certified compliance got a 20 percent larger research tax credit. It also tightened the rules, barring personal importation of controlled substances and requiring destruction without notice of illegal shipments under $10,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who buy prescription drugs at U.S. prices, especially seniors and the uninsured, who could fill 90-day prescriptions from vetted foreign exporters. U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers also gain a new legal supply channel, and the FDA gains a fee-funded monitoring program paid for by the exporters themselves.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high U.S. drug prices

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Health and Human Services Secretary to write regulations waiving import restrictions so qualifying drugs can be brought in from registered exporters in Canada immediately, and from Australia, EU and EFTA countries, Japan, and New Zealand after an 18-month safety report [S2][S3].

Individuals could import up to a 90-day supply for personal or family use with a valid U.S. prescription, and the FDA would publish a public list of registered exporters so consumers could tell legitimate sellers from counterfeiters [S2][S3].

Drugs imported this way had to match an FDA-approved drug's active ingredients, dosage form, and strength, and only manufacturers could get a drug's importation stopped, by petitioning with senior-executive certifications that the version sold abroad differs from the U.S. version [S3].

Drug makers that took action to prevent or condition authorized importation would lose their advertising tax deduction, and makers that certified they had not would get a 20 percent increase in the research tax credit — the bill's answer to industry resistance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. prices would face competition from the same drugs sold cheaper abroad. The administrative cost of inspecting exporters and tracking shipments would be paid through user fees charged to the exporters [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The core objection, pressed by the FDA and the administration at the time, was safety: even with registration, monitoring, and anti-counterfeit markings, the government cannot fully verify every drug's history before it reaches a patient, and the bill's own 18-month report requirement acknowledged the need to study effects on counterfeiting and drug integrity [S2][S3].

Manufacturers could respond by limiting the supply they sell into permitted countries, which could shrink Canadian availability and push Canadian regulators to restrict exports — a practical ceiling on the savings that importation can deliver, which is why the bill added tax penalties aimed at exactly that conduct [S3].

The bill also tightened some rules: it repealed the existing personal-use exemption for importing controlled substances and allowed illegal shipments valued under $10,000 to be refused and destroyed without notice to the owner [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a household paying U.S. prices for long-term medications, the potential savings are real and direct, and the bill went further than most importation proposals in building verifiable safeguards rather than simply opening the border. The honest cost is that no safety regime can fully guarantee the integrity of a foreign supply chain, and drug makers' ability to restrict foreign supply could limit how much patients actually save. On balance this was a patient-focused bill whose main cost fell on an industry, not on consumers.

outcome.mechanism: Grassley introduced it and his own Finance Committee never took it up, so it sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Grassley, a Republican from Iowa and chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced the bill on April 8, 2004, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S3][S5].
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: U.S. prices faced no importation competition, and the mechanism they had opposed never advanced. Americans who hoped to buy cheaper foreign-made drugs kept paying U.S. prices.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; as committee chairman, was positioned to advance it but never brought it to a markup.

for.name: AARP and state and local officials running Canadian drug-buying programs
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed legalizing prescription drug importation from Canada during the debate over high drug prices.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and PhRMA
against.what_they_did: Opposed drug importation during this period, arguing it threatened safety and revenues; the bill's tax penalties were written specifically to counter industry actions to block importation.

against.name: Bush administration and Health and Human Services leadership
against.what_they_did: Opposed legalizing drug importation on safety grounds; HHS secretaries in this era declined to certify importation as safe.

against.name: Sen. Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor; opposed importation during this period.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican committee chairman with zero cosponsors, and drug importation in this era cut across both parties, so the record here shows no clear partisan split.

industries.note: Importation would expose their high U.S. prices to competition from the same drugs sold cheaper in Canada and Europe, and the bill would strip the advertising deduction from any manufacturer found to be obstructing importation. Their interest in blocking or discouraging importation ran directly against patients' interest in lower prices [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Canadian and foreign internet pharmacies and exporters
industries.note: The bill created a legal, FDA-registered exporter pathway with published lists and fee-funded oversight, turning an enforcement gray area into a lawful market serving U.S. patients [S2][S3].

Licensed pharmacists and wholesalers are defined as the importers under the bill and could buy qualifying drugs from registered exporters to dispense at lower cost, though they could not handle the drugs mid-shipment [S3].
